doc.title: Derek Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

chapter: Studio work and the Basie connection
title: Breaking into studio work through Hank Jones's absence; reading
summary: Substituting for a sick Hank Jones got him into jingles and record dates; he stresses reading anything.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: You know there’s been so many stories about these kinds of things where people, Al Grey who happened to be a club when the Basie band was there and their trombone player was sick and the guy said, “get your horn” and he ran, and it’s just little amazing coincidences that helped people.

Well I mean those things work. And I mean that’s, as time goes by, now I’m starting to get a footing, and people say, hey, the kid can play, he speaks kind of weird but he can play, so we’ll hire him. And now, that’s how I got into the studio business. You know what I mean by the studio — playing jingles and record dates and things like that. There was a big band jingle going on, I forget what it was, for what product. But Hank Jones was supposed to be there and for some reason Hank was sick or something and didn’t tell them and he didn’t show up. And there was I downstairs in the bar just hanging out, and they said, “oh the kid’s down there, get that English kid.” And I came in, and I was full of it, and I played my ass off, and they said “okay, the kid’s fine.” And I never looked back. I got in on Hank’s coattail.
That’s where that reading too, comes in important, because you can’t just walk into a studio.

Well that’s where your background comes. I mean if you’ve gone to the academy — there’s no shortcut to reading, you just do it, you just do it. And there’s no shortcut. But the point is when you’re at that stage, when everything is new, read anything. I always tell kids to do that. Read anything. It doesn’t matter what it is. Read saxophone parts. Read anything. Just so that it becomes second nature to you. It’s like breathing.
